title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks (Comprehensive)
author: Maya Patel
body:
Summary

This document consolidates the serving runtime reference material: runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite guidance, release notes summary, known issues, operational runbooks, and team wiki links. It is intended as the canonical high-level + operational reference for engineers who onboard to the serving-runtime team, for SREs performing incident response, and for platform/product stakeholders validating runtime behavior.

Table of contents
1. Introduction and goals
2. Runtime architecture overview
3. Kernel scheduling model and policies
4. Profiling and performance playbook
5. Benchmarking suite and standard measurements
6. Release notes (last three releases)
7. Known issues and mitigations
8. Runtime runbooks (incidents and day-2 ops)
9. Team wiki & onboarding checklist
10. Ownership and escalation

1) Introduction and goals
- Purpose: Provide a single, consumable reference for how Redwood's serving runtime is designed, profiled, benchmarked, and operated in production.
- Audience: serving runtime engineers, infra/SRE, platform, and partner/product engineers integrating models.
- Goals: predictable latency, cost-efficient throughput, graceful degradation, and reproducible performance troubleshooting.

2) Runtime architecture overview
High-level components (logical):
- Ingress/API router: Accepts requests, enforces auth/quota, and applies routing policies (region, cost tier, model variant).
- Request planner: Builds execution plan including KV cache lookups, batching window, and early-exit heuristics.
- Scheduler: Maps execution plans to worker pools (GPU/CPU/quantized fastpath). Implements prioritization and preemption.
- Worker process (executor): Runs the optimized kernels, manages KV cache (per-request & persistent), and streams tokens back via network I/O.
- Observability/metrics exporter: Emits trace spans, token-level cost logs, and detailed GPU counters to the observability stack.
- Control plane: Model catalog, rollout policies, autoscaling controller, and rollback/canary framework.

Key design principles:
- Separation of concerns: planning vs execution vs control plane to minimize tail coupling.
- Workload-aware paths: latency-first vs throughput-first pools with explicit kernel selection.
- Failover and graceful degradation: automatic fallback to compatible model variants and region rerouting.
- Deterministic batching: bounded batching windows and workload-aware batching to keep 99th percentile latency stable.

Operational SLOs and targets (applies to hosted and dedicated):
- P99 tail latency (token emit): 250 ms for short-form generative endpoints (seq_length <= 128).
- P95 latency: 80 ms.
- Availability (platform): 99.95% monthly for hosted inference.
- Error rate (5xxs): < 0.1% of requests.
- Token-level correctness regressions: detect within 1 hour via continuous evals.

3) Kernel scheduling model and policies
Overview:
The scheduler decides: which worker pool, which kernel variant, batch size to use, and whether to route to quantized fastpath. The model supports per-model kernel families and per-queue policies. Scheduling decisions are made using rules + cost model + short-term telemetry.

Scheduling priorities and queues:
- Latency priority queue: for low-latency customers / routes. Max batch size = 8, batching window = 3 ms, preemption = true.
- Balanced queue: default for most routes. Max batch size = 32, batching window = 10 ms, preemption = conditional.
- Bulk throughput queue: for embeddings and batch scoring. Max batch size = 256, batching window = 50 ms, preemption = false.

Kernel selection heuristics:
1. If model is quantization-compatible and route permits, prefer quantized kernel variant (INT8/FP8) for reduced GPU memory and improved throughput.
2. For sequence lengths > 1024, prefer memory-optimized kernels with hierarchical attention fallback where available.
3. If per-request KV cache hit rate > 75% for a route, enable KV-cache-specialized kernel to avoid re-computation of key-value matrices.
4. On GPU utilization > 85% and increased latency, switch new incoming requests to lower-priority throughput pool and enable autoscaling signal.

Preemption and fairness:
- Long-running bulk jobs can be preempted by latency-priority traffic when preemption is enabled for that queue; preemption uses a cooperative checkpoint/restore at attention layer boundaries.
- Fairness across tenants: weighted fair share based on commit tier, with safeguards to prevent noisy neighbor effects.

Configuration examples (sample YAML used by scheduler control plane):
- scheduler_policy: latency_first
- max_batch_size: 32
- batching_window_ms: 10
- quantization_allowed: true
- kv_cache_policy: enable_if_hit_rate_above_0.5

4) Profiling and performance playbook
Purpose: standardize how engineers collect, analyze, and triage performance issues. This section is a step-by-step playbook.

Pre-flight checklist:
- Reproduce issue in staging using the same model and sequence distribution.
- Ensure debug-level traces enabled for a short window (no more than 15 minutes for production).
- Reserve GPU node for profiling to avoid impacting tenant traffic.

Profiling steps:
1. Collect request traces and spans (ingress -> planner -> scheduler -> executor -> exporter). Capture sample payloads.
2. GPU-level profiling: run NVTX/Nsight sampling for kernel durations and memory ops. Capture per-kernel launch latency and SM utilization.
3. Runtime metrics: token latency histograms, batch sizes, queue wait times, KV cache hit/miss ratios, and memory pressure evictions.
4. System metrics: PCIe saturation, host CPU steal, and NIC flow-control events.
5. Heap and GC profiling for Python-managed parts of executor (if using Python control flow).

Analysis workflow:
- Correlate P99 latency spikes with queue wait times and batch sizes to distinguish batching-induced tails vs kernel stalls.
- If GPU occupancy is low but kernel latency high, inspect kernel choice (wrong algorithmic path).
- High PCIe time in combination with small batches suggests frequent KV cache transfers; recommend enabling local GPU-side KV cache.
- Use flamegraphs for executor CPU thread hotspots.

Automated profiling tools and commands (examples):
- capture traces: ./tools/capture_trace --trace-id <id> --duration 60s --filter "route:chat-v2"
- nvprof/Nsight: nsys profile -o /tmp/profile --trace=nvtx --sample=cpu --duration=60 ./bin/executor --config conf.yaml
- dump runtime metrics: curl -s http://executor:8080/metrics | tee /tmp/metrics.txt

Postmortem checklist:
- Document root cause, actions taken, and revert/fix plan. Add summary to incident tracker and notify affected customers.

5) Benchmarking suite and standard measurements
Bench goals: measure steady-state throughput, cold-start latency, tail latency under realistic mix, and per-token cost. The benchmarking harness is in repo: infra/benchmarks/serving-harness.

Standard benchmarks (run weekly and on every runtime release):
- micro-bench: per-kernel latency and memory utilization across sequence lengths [16, 64, 256, 1024, 2048].
- latency-mix: 80/20 interactive/generation mix reflecting typical product traffic. Measures P50/P95/P99 pre- and post-optimization.
- throughput-batch: maximum sustained tokens/sec at target 95th latency.
- kv-cache-effectiveness: measure end-to-end improvements with local KV cache enabled vs disabled.

Benchmarking methodology notes:
- Use representative model artifacts (fp16 baseline + quantized variants).
- Run three warmup runs and five measured trials, take median.
- Use isolated nodes where no other tenants run during measurement.
- Record environment: driver version, CUDA/cuDNN, kernel build, and model commit hash.

Standard metrics captured:
- tokens_per_second, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, gpu_utilization_percent, mem_used_mb, power_watts, cost_per_1M_tokens_usd.

How to run a standard benchmark (example):
- checkout infra/benchmarks/serving-harness
- ./run_benchmark --suite latency-mix --model gpt-lite-7b --replicas 4 --out results/latency-mix-2026-03-03.json

6) Release notes (summary, last three releases)
Release 2026-02-20 (v1.27.0):
- Kernel: added INT8 matmul fastpath for common decoder blocks (avg +18% throughput for small batches).
- Scheduler: new fairness weight scheme for reserved capacity customers.
- Observability: token-level cost exporter added.
- Migration notes: quantized model artifacts require rebuild of model shard index.

Release 2026-01-07 (v1.26.2):
- Bugfix: fixed KV cache eviction causing corrupted attention state under heavy preemption.
- Performance: improved batching heuristics resulting in 6% lower P95 on balanced workloads.

Release 2025-11-15 (v1.25.0):
- Feature: per-route latency SLO annotations and automatic route-level scaling triggers.
- Ops: added benchmarking harness into CI to run nightly smoke tests.

Upgrade guidance:
- Follow the canary rollout checklist in section 8. Always run benchmark suite on canary nodes and compare to baseline. If P99 regresses by >5% or tokens/sec drops by >7%, rollback and open a perf regression ticket.

7) Known issues and mitigations (current)
- Issue: occasional P99 spikes on long-sequence (>1024) chat sessions.
  - Symptom: P99 token latency spikes with batch size = 1 and GPU occupancy low.
  - Mitigation: enable memory-optimized kernel path and increase batching window to 20 ms for that route. Patch scheduled in v1.28.
- Issue: KV cache warmup causes initial token latency bumps on first requests after scale-up.
  - Mitigation: prefill KV cache during scale-up using synthetic warmed requests.
- Issue: rare 500s caused by host OOM during concurrent host-side preprocessing for large batches.
  - Mitigation: limit host preprocess concurrency to 4 and move heavier steps to GPU-side fused kernels.

8) Runtime runbooks (incidents and day-2 ops)
Runbook: P99 tail latency spike (short-form generation)
- Trigger: alert p99_token_latency > 250 ms for 5 minutes for a route
- Owner: oncall-serving-runtime (primary)
- Steps:
  1. Run ./tools/capture_trace --trace-id incident-<ts> --duration 120s --filter "route:<route>" to capture telemetry.
  2. Check queue lengths: curl -s http://scheduler:9090/queues | jq '.routes["<route>"]'
  3. Inspect batch sizes: curl -s http://executor:8080/stats | grep batch_size_distribution
  4. If batch_size == 1 and queue_wait_ms > 10ms, change queue policy for route to increase batching_window_ms to 20 (temporary): \n     POST http://control-plane:8200/api/v1/route-configs/<route>/patch \n     body: {"batching_window_ms":20} (use control-plane CLI to avoid RBAC failures).
  5. If GPU kernel latency is the cause, check recent deployment: git rev-parse HEAD of model + runtime. If new runtime deployed in last 1 hour, rollback to previous canary.
  6. Notify customers via #status-channel if >10% requests affected.

Runbook: GPU node degradation (high ECC or hardware error)
- Trigger: GPU ECC error rate > threshold or nvml reports ECC events
- Owner: infra-sre / serving-runtime primary
- Steps:
  1. Remove node from autoscaling group: ./infra/remove_node --node <id>
  2. Drain node: ./infra/drain_node --node <id> --grace 120
  3. Reprovision replacement with same instance type and rerun benchmarking-sanity.

Canary / rollout checklist (short)
1. Create canary pool (2-4 nodes) with new runtime image.
2. Route 1% traffic for 30 minutes, collect benchmark suite and error traces.
3. Run benchmark suite and compare against baseline. Gate: no P99 regression > 5%, tokens/sec drop > 7%, error rate increase > 0.05%.
4. Gradually increase to 10%, 25%, 50%, 100% with manual approvals and automated metrics checks.

9) Team wiki & onboarding checklist
- Core repos: runtime/executor, runtime/scheduler, infra/benchmarks/serving-harness, observability/metrics-exporter.
- Onboarding tasks (first 2 weeks):
  1. Read this handbook and run local profiler examples.
  2. Run the micro-bench on a small GPU dev node.
  3. Shadow an oncall rotation and review two postmortems.
  4. Complete the kernel-scheduling design review walkthrough with an owner.
- Useful links: design ADRs, kernel selection heuristics doc, benchmarking dashboards (Grafana link: grafana.internal.redwood/services/serving-runtime).

10) Ownership and escalation
- Primary owners: serving-runtime team (listed in OWNERS file): Maya Patel (lead), Connor Beck (scheduler lead), Anika Rao (observability).
- Oncall: serving-runtime oncall rotation (pagerduty: #serving-runtime-oncall).
- Escalation path: oncall -> team lead -> infra-sre -> CTO on critical incidents.

Appendix: useful CLI snippets and config templates
- capture traces: ./tools/capture_trace --trace-id <id> --duration 60s --filter "route:chat-v2"
- run benchmarks: ./run_benchmark --suite latency-mix --model <model> --out <path>
- sample scheduler patch (control-plane CLI): rcp patch-route --route <route> --set batching_window_ms=20 --set max_batch_size=16

Change log (doc): 2026-02-28 initial draft merged; 2026-03-03 added canary checklist and recent release notes.

If you have questions or need handoffs, ping the serving-runtime #team channel or leave a comment on this page.
